newsitem.title: USA: FTC staff asks for new look at "Joe Camel" ads.
newsitem.headline: FTC staff asks for new look at "Joe Camel" ads.

text.p: Federal Trade Commission staff members have asked the commissioners to act against R.J. Reynolds because new evidence shows the tobacco company's "Joe Camel" campaign targets children, a spokeswoman said Wednesday.

The commission voted 3-2 against taking action against the "Joe Camel" campaign in 1994. Last July, Representative Tim Roemer, an Indiana Democrat, and a bipartisan group of 66 other House members asked the FTC to reopen the case.
"We received the petition," said FTC spokeswoman Victoria Streitfeld. "The staff understook an investigation. I can confirm that they are recommending to the commission that they bring a complaint."
The recommendation was first reported in The Wall Street Journal.
A commission vote is expected within the next month or two, and someone familiar with the views of the commissioners said there was a greater chance of getting a positive vote this time.
"There is new evidence that the staff is presenting to the commission, but I cannot comment on what that new evidence is," Streitfeld said. Roemer said he knew what the new evidence was.

"New studies in medical journals ... make more of a direct link between advertising and children," Roemer said in an interview. "There's no way you can convince me that Joe Camel is a symbol and logo to try and get 52-year-olds interested in pool and motorcycles and saxophones so that they smoke."
But in a statement, R.J. Reynolds said the information was not new, pointing to a poll released by the Roper organisation in February 1994.
Roemer's letter cites an October 1995 study in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute, along with others, that came after the FTC decision.
In addition, Roemer said new evidence had been handed over to the FTC from the Food and Drug Administration.
Roemer also said a recent settlement under which Liggett has acknowledged it targeted children in its advertising may also help make the case.
